title: Stuck On You
full_review:
A pair of small-town conjoined twins go Hollywood in the surprisingly tender screwball comedy "Stuck On You" (20th Century Fox).

Conjoined in their creativity, sibling directors Peter and Bobby Farrelly rein in the crass scatological humor exhibited in "Dumb and Dumber" (1994) and "There's Something About Mary" (1998), grafting positive messages about filial fealty and self-esteem onto the film's Siamese slapstick silliness.

Matt Damon and Greg Kinnear play joined-at-the-side brothers, Bob and Walt Tenor, two New England bumpkins who own a burger joint in Martha's Vineyard, where their Kali-limbed hash-slinging and athletic prowess have made them local legends. What hockey team wouldn't want a four-armed goalie?

The fact that Kinnear is noticeably older than Damon is cleverly explained by the fact that Bob (Damon) was born with the lion's share of their collective liver. But blood proves thicker than bile, and together they have learned to use their disability to their advantage.

However, their unconditional support for each other is tested when limelight-longing Walt, drawn by the siren song of Hollywood, decides to pursue his dream of acting, and convinces his socially inept brother to tag along for the ride -- as if he had a choice.

Once in Tinseltown they befriend a ditsy starlet-wannabe (Eva Mendes) who hooks Walt up with an agent (Seymour Cassel), a geriatric huckster whose circa-1970s couture and negotiation skills are stuck in a polyester time warp, and whose idea of a prime gig is getting Walt a part in a porn movie.

Through a seeming stroke of luck, Walter lands a plum role on a prime-time TV series opposite Cher (playing herself). Unbeknownst to Walter, his hiring is part of Cher's plan to sabotage the show's chance of success so she can get out of her contract. Ripping a page out of "The Producers," the show becomes a huge hit, setting Walt on a most unlikely fast lane to fame and fortune. But Walt's newfound celebrity only confirms for Bob that his own small-town sensibilities are weighing his brother down -- literally. The two Tenors make a decision to be surgically separated -- only to discover that their true bond was of the heart, not the hip.

Needless to say, for the film's quirky conceit to work the story must draw viewers beyond the visual eccentricity of its protagonists, or else it remains a sporadically funny but tedious series of punch lines to a one-joke sight gag. In addition to believing that Damon and Kinnear are brothers, it is essential that their characters are likable and worthy of emotional investment. The Farrellys accomplish this by keeping the tenor -- or Tenors -- positive, portraying Bob and Walt not as societal losers but as perennial winners. In fact, they come across as the most "normal" characters in the film.

And while their physical handicap obviously fuels much of the humor, the Farrellys refrain from sharpening lighthearted lampooning into mean-spiritedness or exploitation. The sole exception is an unnecessary scene which wrings cheap laughs out of showing the obstacle their impairment poses to sexual intimacy.

The film's normalizing of people with disabilities extends to those in supporting roles, who, though frequently fair game in Farrelly fare, are never targeted as the brunt of cruel jokes. In fact, the Farrellys frequently populate their cinematic landscapes with real-life physically or mentally challenged people as a means of softening the stigma associated with being perceived as "handicapped" (their next project has the support of the Special Olympics).

And while viewers may justifiably find the Farrellys' brand of humor tasteless at times, "Stuck on You" ultimately imparts a life-affirming message about family and friendship, which, as in the Farrellys' "Shallow Hal" (2001), invites viewers to look past surface superficialities and see each person -- no matter how strange -- as a unique gift and worthy of love. In the end, it reminds us that, as Christians and members of the human family, we are all interconnected at the heart and called to share our lives, if not livers.

Due to recurring sexually crude humor and language, an off-screen sexual encounter and brief alcohol abuse, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
